title: Entropy of a gas that splits in two

stimulus.title: N₂O₄ before and after
stimulus.html:
Colorless N₂O₄(g) breaks apart into brown NO₂(g) in a sealed container at constant temperature: N₂O₄(g) → 2 NO₂(g). ΔH° = +57.2 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +175.8 J/(mol·K).

Key: two joined dark circles, one N₂O₄ molecule; one dark circle, one NO₂ molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the particle diagram, justify the positive sign of ΔS° for the reaction.

rubric.point: Each N₂O₄ molecule becomes two NO₂ molecules, so the number of gas particles increases (4 → 6 in the diagram) and there are more ways to arrange them (more microstates)
accept: more moles of gas, more microstates
more independent gas particles; "disorder" alone does not earn the point

parts.sample: Each N₂O₄ molecule that reacts becomes two NO₂ molecules, so the box goes from 4 to 6 gas particles. More independent gas particles can be arranged in more ways, so there are more microstates and ΔS° > 0.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate ΔG° for the reaction at 298 K.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the temperature above which the reaction is thermodynamically favored.
parts.sample: Set ΔG° = 0: T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 57,200 J/mol ÷ 175.8 J/(mol·K) = 325 K. Above 325 K, TΔS° > ΔH° and ΔG° < 0.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student concludes from part (b) that "no NO₂ is present in the container at 298 K." Explain why this conclusion is incorrect.

rubric.point: ΔG° > 0 means K < 1 (about 0.14), not K = 0, so an equilibrium mixture still contains NO₂; with ΔG° close to zero, both gases are present in significant amounts
accept: K is less than 1 but not zero
a small positive ΔG° gives K near 1, so both species are present

parts.sample: A positive ΔG° means K < 1, not K = 0. K = e^(−4810/(8.314 × 298)) ≈ 0.14, so at equilibrium the container holds mostly N₂O₄ but also a significant amount of NO₂; ΔG° is close to zero, so both are present.
